claims.text: A data-driven machine-learning workflow can identify and optimize multi-step processing and thermal-treatment paths for multi-phase alloys.
Such ML-optimized paths can simultaneously enhance phase stability, refine microstructure, and improve mechanical properties.
Conventionally produced multi-phase or high-entropy alloys exhibit heterogeneous phase distributions.
Conventionally produced multi-phase or high-entropy alloys have relatively coarse microstructures.
Conventional high-entropy-alloy processing can involve multiple casting, rolling, homogenization, and annealing steps.
The proposed optimization varies heat-treatment temperature profiles, cooling rates, and hold times.
The processing-parameter window can be determined from available experimental data.
ML-guided processing will produce a more uniform and refined microstructure.
ML-guided processing will produce stable phase configurations.
Computational and data-driven tools can screen a large alloy-design space and investigate composition and temperature effects on microstructure.
An ML workflow can screen the processing-structure-property space to predict optimized thermal and thermomechanical treatments.
Applying ML-predicted processing parameters promotes the formation of stable phases.
Applying ML-predicted processing parameters promotes grain refinement.
Stable phases and grain refinement lead to enhanced mechanical properties.
ML-optimized processing will increase strength and ductility relative to conventional processing.
Heuristically selected conventional processing parameters often cause phase instability, coarse grains, or strength-ductility trade-offs.
The effectiveness of the ML workflow depends on the quality and extent of its training data.
The complexity and size of the alloy processing-design space can limit optimization and create a need for efficient design tools.
The magnitude of improvement will vary with alloy system and processing-parameter space.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements over a conventionally processed control would falsify the hypothesis.
